finding: Share of world population living in autocracies at end-2025
citation: V-Dem Institute (2026). Democracy Report 2026. University of Gothenburg
notes: Report text: '74% of the world population (6 billion) now live in autocracies'. Downloaded PDF and extracted text.

finding: Autocracies vs democracies at end-2025; share in liberal democracies
citation: V-Dem Institute (2026). Democracy Report 2026. University of Gothenburg
notes: '92 autocracies and 87 democracies'; 'Only 7% ... live in liberal democracies'. 2025 edition gave 91/88.

finding: Countries autocratizing in 2025
citation: V-Dem Institute (2026). Democracy Report 2026. University of Gothenburg
notes: 'Nearly a quarter of the world's nations ... 44 countries'; 10 new autocratizers in 2025.

finding: Share of world population living in autocratizing countries
citation: V-Dem Institute (2026). Democracy Report 2026. University of Gothenburg
notes: Described as a record.

finding: Media censorship is the most common tactic of autocratizing governments
citation: V-Dem Institute (2026). Democracy Report 2026. University of Gothenburg
notes: Repression of civil society: 30 countries (68%). Supports scenario 11 (information monopoly).

finding: Freedom of expression declining vs 2015; 'often the first domino to fall'
citation: V-Dem Institute (2026). Democracy Report 2026. University of Gothenburg
notes: In 2000 only 5 countries were limiting and 52 expanding freedom of expression.

finding: Coup attempts 1950-2015 in Powell & Thyne data (version 2015.09.30)
citation: Powell & Thyne (2011). Global instances of coups from 1950 to 2010: A new dataset. Journal of Peace Research 48(2):249-259. doi:10.1177/0022343310397436; counts from dataset as packaged in AuthoritarianismBook R package
notes: Counts verified on package documentation page, not on the live dataset (uky.edu returned 403). Roughly half of attempts succeed. Live dataset is updated; later counts differ.

finding: Coup-proofing methods: special loyalties, parallel militaries, internal security agencies; cost is reduced military power
citation: Quinlivan (1999). Coup-proofing: Its Practice and Consequences in the Middle East. International Security 24(2):131-165. doi:10.1162/016228899560202
notes: Abstract. UNIRA must NOT copy regime coup-proofing (loyalty-based); it uses structural, rule-based dispersion instead.

finding: Ethnic exclusion substitutes civil war risk for coup risk; purged co-conspirators and co-ethnics far more likely to rebel within 3 years
citation: Roessler (2011). The Enemy Within: Personal Rule, Coups, and Civil War in Africa. World Politics 63(2):300-346. doi:10.1017/S0043887111000049
notes: Abstract. Implies the Peace Force must never be stacked with, or purged of, any group; mixing by rule not by loyalty.

finding: Building ethnic armies, or dismantling those of predecessors, provokes violent resistance from officers
citation: Harkness (2016). The Ethnic Army and the State. Journal of Conflict Resolution 60(4):587-616. doi:10.1177/0022002714545332
notes: Abstract. A '<20% to ~89%' coup-risk figure seen in a search snippet was NOT verified and is not used. Relevant to transition (T-5) dissolution of national armies.

finding: Counterbalancing reduces the likelihood that coup attempts succeed (mainly by giving some soldiers incentives to resist) but is not associated with fewer attempts
citation: De Bruin (2018). Preventing Coups d'etat: How Counterbalancing Works. Journal of Conflict Resolution 62(7):1433-1458
notes: Abstract. Supports multi-key and dispersed command plus protected duty to refuse (resistance from inside).

finding: Creation of a new security force increases the odds of a coup attempt in the following year
citation: De Bruin (2018), as above
notes: Abstract. Peace Force build-up is the riskiest period (already noted in Art. 5a.5).

finding: Structural coup-proofing (counterbalancing) and spending found to deter coup activity
citation: Powell (2012). Determinants of the Attempting and Outcome of Coups d'etat. Journal of Conflict Resolution 56(6):1017-1040. doi:10.1177/0022002712445732
notes: Only search-result summary seen, abstract not fetched; De Bruin (2017 WP) reports results significant in only half of specifications. Treat as weak.

finding: Open-ended coups, executive coups and blatant election-day fraud are declining; promissory coups, executive aggrandizement and strategic electoral manipulation are increasing
citation: Bermeo (2016). On Democratic Backsliding. Journal of Democracy 27(1):5-19
notes: Abstract. Main threat is a lawful-looking, gradual erosion by elected leaders, not tanks. The 35%->85% promissory-coup figure was NOT verified.

finding: Share of presidents reaching end of term (since 2000) who attempted to stay in office
value: at least one-third (about half excluding strongest democracies)
citation: Versteeg, Horley, Meng, Guim & Guirguis (2020). The Law and Politics of Presidential Term Limit Evasion. Columbia Law Review 120(1):173
notes: Based on 234 incumbents in 106 countries.

finding: Evasion attempts that involved amending the constitution
citation: Versteeg, Horley, Meng, Guim & Guirguis (2020). The Law and Politics of Presidential Term Limit Evasion. Columbia Law Review 120(1):173
notes: Supports entrenching term limits beyond ordinary amendment, and a no-benefit-to-incumbent rule.

finding: Evasion attempts that failed
citation: Versteeg, Horley, Meng, Guim & Guirguis (2020). The Law and Politics of Presidential Term Limit Evasion. Columbia Law Review 120(1):173
notes: Implies roughly two-thirds succeeded. Authors: popular resistance more effective than courts.

finding: Attempts to delay elections succeeded
citation: Versteeg, Horley, Meng, Guim & Guirguis (2020). The Law and Politics of Presidential Term Limit Evasion. Columbia Law Review 120(1):173
notes: Supports a fixed, non-postponable election date (eternity clause).

finding: Courts played a role in successful overstays
citation: Versteeg, Horley, Meng, Guim & Guirguis (2020). The Law and Politics of Presidential Term Limit Evasion. Columbia Law Review 120(1):173
notes: Courts can be captured and used to legalise evasion; Court independence must be designed in, not assumed.

finding: Executives observe term limits with remarkable frequency in consolidated democracies; evasion mostly by amending or replacing the constitution
citation: Ginsburg, Melton & Elkins (2011). On the Evasion of Executive Term Limits. William & Mary Law Review 52(6):1807
notes: Abstract. Authors argue clarity of term limits aids enforceability.

finding: Only half of national constitutions (1789-2005) live more than nineteen years; design can lower the risk of death substantially
citation: Elkins, Ginsburg & Melton (2009). The Endurance of National Constitutions. Cambridge University Press
notes: Cline Center summary page. A world constitution should expect pressure to replace it; the replacement route itself must be protected.

finding: Established independent judiciaries prevent regime changes toward authoritarianism across all types of states
citation: Gibler & Randazzo (2011). Testing the Effects of Independent Judiciaries on the Likelihood of Democratic Backsliding. American Journal of Political Science 55(3):696-709. doi:10.1111/j.1540-5907.2010.00504.x
notes: Abstract.

finding: Newly formed courts are positively associated with regime collapses in both democracies and nondemocracies
citation: Gibler & Randazzo (2011), as above
notes: A new world Court will be weakest in its first years: protect its budget, size and jurisdiction from day one.

finding: Democracies more likely to erode under a state of emergency (60 democracies, 1974-2016)
citation: Lührmann & Rooney (2020). Autocratization by Decree: States of Emergency and Democratic Decline. V-Dem Working Paper 2020:85 2nd ed.; published Comparative Politics 53(4) 2021
notes: Working paper abstract (2nd ed., April 2020). Published journal version not fetched; figure may differ (an earlier version said 59%). Association, not proven causation.

finding: Emergency provisions that mandate termination within a specific time frame; provisions granting decrees with force of law
citation: Lührmann & Rooney (2020). Autocratization by Decree: States of Emergency and Democratic Decline. V-Dem Working Paper 2020:85 2nd ed.; published Comparative Politics 53(4) 2021
notes: Supports hard time limit and ban on decrees changing the constitution.

finding: Autocratization episodes in democracies 1974-2016; episodes ending in breakdown of democracy
citation: Lührmann & Rooney (2020). Autocratization by Decree: States of Emergency and Democratic Decline. V-Dem Working Paper 2020:85 2nd ed.; published Comparative Politics 53(4) 2021
notes: Most autocratization episodes starting in democracies ended in breakdown.

finding: Canada 2022: Federal Court (Mosley J, Jan 2024) held the Emergencies Act invocation unreasonable and the order to freeze accounts and disclose financial information violated Charter s.8 (unreasonable search and seizure)
citation: Canada (Federal Court) 2024, Canadian Civil Liberties Association v. Canada (Mosley J); reported in The Hub, 24 Jan 2024
notes: Verified via press paraphrase, not the judgment. Government appealed; outcome of appeal not checked. A figure of 280 frozen accounts seen in a search snippet was NOT verified.

finding: German Basic Law Art. 79(3): amendments affecting division into Länder, Länder participation in legislation, or principles of Art. 1 and 20 are inadmissible
citation: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany, Art. 79(3) (official English translation)
notes: Model for Article 42a. Art. 79(2): two-thirds of Bundestag and two-thirds of Bundesrat.

finding: German Basic Law Art. 20(4): right to resist anyone seeking to abolish the constitutional order if no other remedy is available
citation: Basic Law, Art. 20(4)
notes: Model for protected refusal of unlawful orders (Article 5c).

finding: Share of constitutions with unamendable provisions: 1789-1944 17%; 1945-1988 27%; 1989-2013 53%
citation: Roznai, Y. Towards a Theory of Constitutional Unamendability (Jus Politicum); see also Roznai (2017) Unconstitutional Constitutional Amendments, OUP
notes: Eternity clauses are now the majority practice in new constitutions. Evidence on whether they actually prevent backsliding is weaker (judgement).

finding: Representative deliberative processes catalogued by OECD
citation: OECD (2020). Innovative Citizen Participation and New Democratic Institutions: Catching the Deliberative Wave. OECD Publishing
notes: Quoted on newDemocracy summary page; OECD full report not fetched directly. 12 distinct models identified.

finding: Examples where deliberation is institutionalised; Ostbelgien permanent Citizens' Council
unit: examples / citizens selected by civic lottery with agenda-setting power
citation: OECD (2020), as above
notes: Permanent lottery-based bodies exist at regional scale; not yet at world scale.

finding: Irish Citizens' Assembly: 99 randomly selected citizens plus chair; 87% of members agreed the abortion provision should not be retained in full
citation: Electoral Reform Society (29 May 2018). The Irish abortion referendum: how a Citizens Assembly helped to break years of political deadlock
notes: Assembly 2016-18 covered 5 topics.

finding: Irish referendum on the Thirty-sixth Amendment (25 May 2018), following the Assembly's recommendation
citation: IFES ElectionGuide: Ireland Referendum 2018
notes: No: 723,632 (33.60%). Turnout about 64% (own calculation from 2,159,655 cast / 3,367,556 registered). Shows lot-based assemblies can unlock decisions elected bodies avoided; not evidence that they stop capture.

finding: Politically controlled central banks more likely to produce high and variable inflation; little evidence of effect on real growth (16 OECD countries)
citation: Alesina & Summers (1993). Central Bank Independence and Macroeconomic Performance. Journal of Money, Credit and Banking 25(2):151-162
notes: Abstract. Later studies question robustness. Transfers by analogy only: the U has fixed prices, so the risk is political manipulation of the cap, not inflation.

finding: Discretionary policy can be inferior to committed rules even with agreed objectives (time inconsistency)
citation: Kydland & Prescott (1977). Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans. Journal of Political Economy 85(3):473-492. doi:10.1086/260580
notes: Citation verified from PDF identifier; abstract text came from search snippets only (PDF is a scan). Basis for a rule-bound Monetary Authority.

finding: ECB digital euro design: offline payments with cash-like privacy; online, Eurosystem uses pseudonymisation, hashing and encryption so it cannot directly link transactions to specific users
citation: ECB (24 June 2024). Press release: ECB publishes first progress report on digital euro preparation phase
notes: Design intent, not deployed system. Shows a public digital currency can be built so the issuer cannot see who paid whom.

finding: ECB digital euro holdings would be subject to holding limits and earn no interest
citation: ECB (2024), as above
notes: A EUR 3,000 limit has been discussed in press but is NOT an ECB decision (not verified).

finding: BIS Project Tourbillon (with Swiss National Bank): eCash prototypes giving cash-like anonymity to the payer; quantum-safe crypto raised payment time about 5x and cut throughput by a factor of 200
citation: BIS Innovation Hub Swiss Centre & Swiss National Bank (2023). Project Tourbillon
notes: Payer anonymity is technically feasible; payees (merchants) remain identifiable for compliance. Prototype only.

finding: Permissive Action Links prevent unauthorized arming or detonation; NSAM 160 (June 1962) ordered PALs in all US nuclear weapons in Europe; two-man rule prevents launch by a single individual
citation: Wikipedia: Permissive action link (secondary; cites NSAM 160)
notes: Secondary source. Precedent for weapons that physically cannot be used without codes held by different people (multi-key).

finding: US DOE two-person concept: at least two authorized persons present during all operations giving access to a nuclear explosive, to prevent accidental or unauthorized action
citation: US DOE Order 5610.11, Chapter III (Two-Person Concept), mirrored by FAS
notes: Older DOE order (mirror). Principle generalises to heavy weapons under multi-region keys.

finding: Ethiopia Constitution Art. 39(4): secession needs two-thirds of the group's legislative council, a federal referendum within three years, majority vote, transfer of powers, and division of assets as prescribed by law
citation: Constitution of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia (1995), Art. 39(4)
notes: Text verified. Effects (never used; Tigray conflict 2020-22) NOT verified here; a clear legal exit right did not by itself prevent armed conflict.

finding: EU Treaty Art. 50: any Member State may withdraw in accordance with its own constitutional requirements; Treaties cease to apply on the withdrawal agreement or two years after notification unless unanimously extended
citation: Treaty on European Union, Art. 50 (consolidated, legislation.gov.uk)
notes: Model for a default exit date so the centre cannot block exit by stalling. UK is the only state to have used it (not re-verified here).

finding: Nevis 1998 secession referendum: 61.7% in favour, short of the two-thirds required by section 113 of the St Kitts and Nevis Constitution
citation: Forum of Federations (July 2026). Policy Brief: Saint Kitts and Nevis - Secessionism and the Federal Experience
notes: Other sources give 61.83% (2,427 yes / 1,498 no). Shows a supermajority threshold can keep a unit in despite a clear majority; the vote was peaceful and lawful.

finding: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) prohibits AI social scoring leading to detrimental treatment; Art. 5(1)(d) prohibits predicting a person's criminal risk based solely on profiling
citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Art. 5
notes: Secondary site reproducing the regulation text. Model for 'AI never decides sanctions; no social scoring'.

finding: Dutch childcare benefits: tax authority algorithm built risk profiles of applicants; nationality was a risk factor, resulting in discrimination and racial profiling
citation: Amnesty International (2021). Xenophobic Machines (EUR 35/4686/2021)
notes: Counts of ~20,000-26,000 families and the January 2021 cabinet resignation are widely reported but NOT verified in fetched text here.

finding: UNIRA draft: Coordination Council (executive) currently deploys the Peace Force (Art. 5a.2); no emergency article; no Monetary Authority; no media article; Art. 42 amendment rule not itself entrenched
citation: UNIRA Constitution Draft 1 (v75)
notes: Internal reading, used in the stress test.

finding: UNIRA Peace Force ceiling and plan
citation: UNIRA Constitution Draft 1, Art. 5a.4
notes: Internal. About 12 per 100,000 people at ceiling.
